# The Biology of Lactoferrin, an Iron-Binding Protein That Can Help Defend Against Viruses and Bacteria
@article{Kell2020TheBO, title={The Biology of Lactoferrin, an Iron-Binding Protein That Can Help Defend Against Viruses and Bacteria}, author={Douglas B. Kell and Eugene L. Heyden and Etheresia Pretorius}, journal={Frontiers in Immunology}, year={2020}, volume={11}, url={https://api.semanticscholar.org/CorpusID:218973342} }
There is evidence that lactoferrin can bind to at least some of the receptors used by coronaviruses and thereby block their entry, and may consequently be of preventive and therapeutic value during the present COVID-19 pandemic.
...
This narrative review aims to highlight the most relevant findings concerning LF’s anti-viral, anti-microbial, iron-binding, immunomodulatory, microbiota-modulatory and intestinal barrier properties that support health of the two most affected organs in COVID-19 patients (lungs and gut), and explore the possible underlying mechanisms governing its mode of action.
...
It is proposed that LF can be a possible prophylactic or therapeutic agent for COVID-19 disease, a major cause of atypical pneumonia worldwide.
...
Oral administration of LLF increased lactoferrin levels in blood serum and enhanced the expression of LTF, AGT, and GCSF genes while GM-CSF levels remained unchanged, support that LLF activates the innate-immune response and increase the defense system against bacterial and viral infections.
...
It is suggested that lactoferrin functions as a key component of mammalian host defense at the mucosal surface in mice and humans.
...
Lactoferrin is an abundant iron-binding protein in milk that displays a cytokine-like "alarmin" activity, and it activates the immune system, and in doing so, it modulates the activity of the host immune response.
...
Recent in vitro studies indicate that lactoferrin is able to compete with the LPS-binding protein for LPS binding and therefore to prevent the transfer of LPS to CD14 present at the surface of monocytes, which strongly suggest that lact oferrin are one of the key molecules which modulate the inflammatory response.

Human lactoferrin, an iron-binding multifunctional cationic glycoprotein secreted by exocrine glands and by neutrophils, inhibits intracellular iron overload, an unsafe condition enhancing in vivo susceptibility to infections, as well as anemia of inflammation (AI), re-establishing IIH.

In vitro studies have shown that LF is able to prevent viral infection with an effect that is dose-dependent, precisely by acting through the interaction with heparin sulfate glycosaminoglycan cell receptors (HSPGs).
